title: The Fewest Work Sessions

concept.title: The state is the set of finished tasks; keep the best (sessions, load)
body: You have `n` tasks with given durations, and a work session lasts at most `t`. A task must be done completely inside one session. Find the smallest number of sessions. This is *bin packing*: hard in general, but for 14 tasks the state space is small. Whatever order tasks were done in, what matters for the future is only **which tasks are done** (a bit mask), how many sessions were started, and how much time is used in the **last** session.

For every set of done tasks, keep the best pair `(sessions, load)`: fewer sessions is better, and with the same number of sessions, a smaller load in the last session is better (more room left). From a set, add one more task `i`: if it fits into the last session, the load grows; otherwise a new session is opened and the load becomes `a[i]`.

The comparison of two pairs is the comparison of tuples: first the sessions, then the load. Doing the tasks in some order and always keeping the best state for each set of tasks is the idea of **dynamic programming over subsets**: `2^14 * 14` steps instead of the `14!` orders a plain search would explore.

statement: There are `n` tasks; task `i` takes `a[i]` units of time and cannot be split. A work session lasts at most `t` units of time. The tasks of one session are done one after another, and a task must be finished inside one session. Print the smallest number of sessions needed to finish all the tasks.
inputFormat: The second line has the `n` durations.

examples.note: The tasks 2 and 3 fill one session of length 5, and the task 1 goes into a second session. One session is not enough because the total is 6.

hints: Describe the state by the set of finished tasks (a bit mask).
For every state keep the pair (number of sessions, load of the last session) and prefer the smaller pair.
Adding a task either fits in the last session or opens a new one.

starter.python:
n, t = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

explanation: For each set of finished tasks, the best pair (sessions, load of the last session) is kept. Adding a task either fits in the last session or starts a new one. The answer is the session count of the full set.
